title: Trump Brands Michigan Senate Winner El-Sayed a 'Hater of Jews' as Race Takes National Stage
excerpt: The president attacked Democrat Abdul El-Sayed hours after his narrow primary victory over Haley Stevens, casting the Michigan Senate race as a test of progressive versus establishment politics ahead of November.
body:
• Trump called Abdul El-Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel" on Truth Social after El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary
  • El-Sayed, an Egyptian American public health official, won with roughly 48.5% to Stevens's 47.5% — far tighter than pre-election polls predicted
  • The race was defined by Israel and antisemitism debates; El-Sayed supports conditioning U.S. military aid to Israel while Stevens had pro-Israel PAC backing
  • El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in November in a contest that could help determine Senate control

President Donald Trump wasted no time attacking Abdul El-Sayed after the progressive candidate emerged from a razor-thin Democratic Senate primary in Michigan on Wednesday, branding him a "Communist loser who hates Jews" and casting the result as a gift to the Republican Party.

El-Sayed, a former public health official of Egyptian descent, edged out Rep. Haley Stevens by roughly one percentage point — a margin that caught both parties off guard after polls had forecast a comfortable El-Sayed victory. Stevens conceded Wednesday morning and endorsed her former rival.

A Race Defined by Israel

The primary was shaped by the politics of Israel and antisemitism in ways that previewed the likely fault lines of the general election. El-Sayed ran on Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, and ending unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. He has described Israel's operations in Gaza as a genocide and campaigned alongside Hasan Piker, a progressive streamer who has drawn backlash for inflammatory comments about Israel and Jews.

Stevens, the Democratic establishment candidate, drew backing from pro-Israel groups and an endorsement from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

"I believe that we cannot continue to do unconditional foreign military aid. I believe that we have to follow our own laws, the Leahy laws, where we don't sell weaponry to countries that have engaged in human rights abuses."

— Abdul El-Sayed, on MSNBC's Morning Joe

In his victory speech, El-Sayed committed himself to "Jewish safety" and framed his anti-war stance as universal rather than targeted. He said he would take the same position on conditioning aid whether the country in question were Israel or Egypt, where his parents emigrated from.

Trump's Broadside

Trump devoted a substantial portion of a Las Vegas speech Wednesday to attacking El-Sayed, repeating the "hater of Jews" line and calling him "full of s---" in remarks that leaned heavily on casting Democrats as communists.

"The polls were wrong again last night when they thought it would be a landslide victory for a hater of Jews and a hater of Israel," Trump told the crowd. He argued that Republican nominee Mike Rogers — the former FBI director and congressman — would fare better against El-Sayed than he would have against Stevens.

The comments echoed Trump's past attacks against New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he also branded as a communist. Republican strategists see the progressive labels as an opportunity in competitive races.

Michigan's Indian American Dimension

The Michigan Senate race carries particular weight for the Indian American community. El-Sayed's financial disclosures reveal he owns property in Bangalore, India, and Dubai — facts that Republicans have already seized on. The race follows Indian American Rep. Shri Thanedar's loss in the state's 13th Congressional District primary on the same night, marking a significant reshuffling of South Asian and immigrant representation in Michigan politics.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the DSCC quickly endorsed El-Sayed, signaling that Democrats will unite behind the progressive nominee despite internal divisions.

What's Next

El-Sayed faces Rogers in a November contest that both parties see as pivotal for Senate control. The race will test whether Trump's "communist" framing resonates in a battleground state where progressive energy and Arab American voter turnout have reshaped Democratic politics. National spending is expected to be significant from both sides.
nri_angle: El-Sayed owns property in Bangalore; Thanedar's same-night loss reshuffles South Asian representation in Michigan politics.
